utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon to everybody, to the Prosecution bench, to the Defence counsel, to the accused including Mr. Petkovic, and my greetings to the supporting staff. You have the floor for two IC numbers, Mr. Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [French on English channel]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IC 252. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber is going to issue an oral decision regarding the video. We had deliberations this morning and we decided that the video had to be introduced during the testimony of the said witness. Since it is about 58 minutes long, the Trial Chamber urges the Prosecution to reduce as much as possible the end of the direct examination so that the Defence can have at least two hours before the end of the day for cross-examination purposes. Ms. Egels, you have the floor. Please finish your direct examination and then we can have the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to add, because I'd fear don't to say that if later on the Defence were to think that during cross-examination they would not have had the time needed to ask all relevant questions of the witness, the Defence can always file objections in writing pursuant to earlier decisions when there are challenges on evidence. You have the floor, Ms. Egels.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Witness, we left after yesterday after a pretty extensive explanation of what the conditions were at the hospital in East Mostar after 9 May of 1993. I would like to go back to some specifics that you gave us yesterday. You talked about the fact that one of the nurses, Linda, had been killed on the 9th of May. Now, given the location of the hospital and your description of the situation, could you tell the Court if the hospital building itself has been affected by combat activities after the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the way it was: Quite simply put it could be seen in the photographs that were displayed a countless number of times. The building was bullet-riddled with small bullets at that. The roof was hit a countless number of times. We had this man who was just in charge of fixing the roof tiles every day. And I know of two major hits with something that was probably a tank shell or a cannonball. I come to that conclusion because there was this enormous whole on the wall. Not on the roof but on the wall, and I could fit into that hole once I stood there right in front of that hole. And one was on the north or north-east side of the building, and the later one was on the western side of the send part on the central floor, that is to say on the upper floor depending on how you do your counting, downstairs, on the upstairs, the first floor, the second floor, but anyway, both hits were upstairs. At any rate, unfortunately in both cases it was the pharmacies that were hit, our pharmaceutical materials. So a lot of it was destroyed during the first shelling and the second shelling and the same thing happened afterwards as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, the hospital did it have any distinctive markings on it, on the building or surrounding the building showing that it was a hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this big marking that was made of bed sheets because they were put together, and it was very long and there was a red cross in the middle, and that was on the fence on both sides. And since we mostly came in from the left-hand side, as we called it, from the south, that is, I think that that's the one that was the most obvious one. It was this enormous flag, if I can call it that, with the red cross on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Except for Linda, were there any other members of the medical staff that have been the target of fire after the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Doctor Camdzic, an old lady doctor, she got killed. She was seriously wounded, operated on, then later on evacuated to Split, but she died. Dr. Konjhodzic was hit with a shell in the left side of his chest and that is why he could not work. He could not function. For quite a while he was a patient in the hospital. Dr. Rizvanbegovic was hit too. I think that that even exists on the recording that I saw many times. I think it was the BBC video clip when Dr. Rizvanbegovic was wounded. Two nurses got killed who were working there. Anyway, it was relatively near the hygiene department. One was called Sunita and I do not remember the name of the other one. There were some other people who were wounded. We call these people civilian protection, but basically they were just stretcher bearers. Also a person got killed who - well, how shall I put this? - worked on preparing corpses and records of the killed. Agib Morina is his name. He worked in the hospital before the war and during the war he worked with us. He got killed right in front of the hygiene department, and I think it was a big shell that hit him. Possibly there are other casualties as well, but -- oh, yes. There was nurse Sejdifa as well. She was wounded too.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: During your testimony you referred on several occasions to sniping. You referred to victims of sniper fire. Do you have any idea where that sniping fire came from? Did these victims or other people tell you where the sniping fire came from?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have an idea, and I have my very own experience, so I know of at least two points that can be characterised as such. One was called the general high school, and I don't think it's only the building of the general high school. In my view, it's also the buildings that were near the high school. The high school is the central building and next door to it there is an elementary school that's very similar to it, architecturally speaking. And then there is the glass bank as it was called, because it was all in glass, that building. Before, of course. None of that is left. Now, why do I know that? Because from time to time I had to go that way, in that direction where there was sniping. So you'd have to take the main street, Tito Street. Not the street but you had to go through the backyards because there was a sign saying, "Watch out, sniper." For years even after the war there was this sign and you'd have to go all around. And the second place I am referring to, not on the basis of my personal experience but on the basis of what patients told me and -- what my wife told me, for instance, is that locality which was targeted that that is an area that has a threefold name, Luka Tekija. Some people call it one thing some people call it the other thing but it's the very same thing. It is an extension of the Hasan Brkic bridge, and those who were targeting us were on the hillock on the other side called Stotina. That is a very broad area. It is a four-lane street and then there is the sidewalks. So it's an open space and there was no other way of crossing to the other side but taking that risk. There is no other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you now to go to Exhibit number 2791. It is in the first binder just next to you. Yesterday you explained extensively how to read a protocol book that was presented to you under Exhibit number 2786. As you will all see, this exhibit in the hard copy bears a yellow sticker almost in the middle of it. Can I ask you to first start by the first part which is before the yellow sticker and tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first page?

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: It is the first page in your binder. And on e-court it is page number 123 of that document.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same page that we saw last time. As I said, it is one of the last pages of one of the first protocols that had first been started as an outpatient protocol and then it continues as a surgery protocol from the 9th of May, because at that time whatever the diagnosis was, we admitted all our patients into the same room. So that's one of those pages. Dated the 9th of May, by the way. I say I remember that by patient 4545. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Indeed. And flipping through those pages up to the yellow sticker, is this the continuity of that same protocol book you are now referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the pages of the 9th of May. Linda Petrovic is here. I know that for sure. I don't see the first stamp here. We use the stamp to show what day it was. For us it would begin at midnight, and then later on we'd have our shift changes at 8.00. Yes. 10th of May. It's the very same protocol.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: If I can direct you now to the yellow sticker. Could you tell the Trial Chamber what this page is? And that is the first page of the document on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a photocopy of the cover page or the first page, if I should call it that, of the protocol of the war hospital. This is emergencies, surgery. On the 19th of May, 1993 until the 15th of June, 1993. It seems to be a relatively short period, but that's not the point, whether it's a big book or a small book. This protocol, after the 15th of June because of the volume of our work was taken upstairs and continues as the outpatient protocol, because upstairs we had to have an infirmary for these sort of regular cases, peacetime cases if I can call it that whereas in the basement we just had the surgery left. So the new protocol was opened downstairs. I think it started with number 1, whereas this one continues with big numbers. You can see here in the thousands and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Going to the second page of that protocol that starts on the 19th of May, 1993, could you briefly explain to the Trial Chamber what the difference is between that protocol and the first one that we saw?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first difference is in the origin of this protocol. This protocol obviously was intended for some kind of laboratory documentation, because it says here "material," who was sending the material and what material. It's probably the laboratory protocol. We used what we found. We didn't have any specially printed protocols for us. Secondly I told you there was this basic principle from day 1 that we had a date and then later on we did not have ink for the stamp so then we had to write this in hand and then there would be the number of the patient, the name and surname which is obligatory, and then the year of birth and the diagnosis and over here the therapy as well, because there was enough room to write that down as well. Sometime in some places, I believe over here too, there are additional pieces of information like housecalls, if somebody went to the neighbourhood to visit a patient. But anyway, this is the basic data.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to turn to Exhibit number 4287. That is also in that first binder. As you just explained yesterday and today, from the 15th of June onwards there were two separate protocol books that were held at the hospital. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what this protocol book is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photocopy of the first page or, rather, the cover page of this newly established protocol that we used down there in the cellar. It starts on the 15th of June, 1993, and ends on the 18th of August, 1993. On this page it says quite clearly that it's the protocol of the laboratory. That is what it had been intended for but that's not the way it ended up. You can see that judging by the rubrics. I already mentioned that. See, it really starts with number 1. So it's 1, 2, 3, 4. The date is the 15th of June. That is the moment when the protocol was taken upstairs and continued as the infirmary protocol, whereas this one remained surgery only and it has the very same rubrics, and basically the same ones that we established as usual, that is to say name, surname, number, year of birth, and so on. I don't remember having seen this and the other pages, but here, yes. The rubric that is supposed to be affiliation, someone, something for the first patient -- it says the 3rd Battalion, the 2nd Company. Then the second patient is a civilian, the third one is MUP, that is to say a policeman. The fourth one is from the customs company, the Carina company, and then civilians. And the last bit is interesting I think. Sometimes it would be written in one place and sometimes in another place. That is to say where the wounding took place. Fejiceva street, the cinema, and then in parentheses, and then Lero is an old restaurant. So it's on two sides, this protocol. I remember it. What I'm seeing now is the left-hand side of the protocol. On the right-hand side where the diagnoses and the treatment. See, so it's the left-hand side and the right-hand side where the diagnosis is put and what was done. Analgesics and dressing wounds and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: So just for the purpose of the record, when you refer to the left-hand side of the protocol you refer to the first page that you were looking at, and when you refer to the right-hand side of the protocol you refer to the second page of the document that you were looking at?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Do you notice or recognise your own handwriting in that protocol?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Here under number 28, 29, 30. The complete rubric is filled out in my own hand. Also, 25. Well, I'm not doing this in the right order, but, say, the place of wounding, all of it is my handwriting. And it's the neighbourhood on the north-east. And then the block letters are mine, and then the patient number 22 as well. Yeah. If the number is important, 22, 25, 28, 29, 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to turn to Exhibit number 9675, and that is in the second binder next to you. Can I ask you to tell the Trial Chamber what this document is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a photocopy of the first page of the protocol that continues from what we looked at a few moments ago, from the 18th of August until the 13th of October, 1993. Yes, that's it. As far as I can remember, the book is of an identical form like the one that was photocopied before. So on one page you have the left and the right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Would that be just the same type of protocol book but just a continuation in time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to turn to Exhibit number 5853 in the same binder, please? And could you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this side it -- we see a copy of the first page of the emergency surgical ward of the war hospital of the 13th of October, 1993, until the 24th of May, 1994. Here we see the first page, the cover page. Shall we go on?

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Yes, please. The two next pages.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next -- these two pages do not belong to the protocol as such. They are of that provenance, so to speak. This was torn out of a protocol book. I can explain about these two pages in detail if you wish. It's a kind of temperature lists that we kept. Now, why? Usually we would use any empty sheet. Usually it would just be a regular sheet of paper and then we would put a horizontal line, and a vertical line, and then we would put down the basics, name, surname, year of birth, diagnosis in the corner. I cannot see here from the photocopy but, see, there is this part here, diagnosis. And then there's a number, 114, and the number would usually be taken from the protocol onto the temperature list. And then if ever a discharge letter was to be written then that number would be referred to. Then underneath the usual thing, the first day of admission, the 27th of October. That is what it says here. If the patient would remain with us, if the patient survived, then the list would stay. And if the patient would be discharged definitely or if the patient would die, then we'd turn on to the other page. So usually we'd have double writing, trim writing we'd cross things out and go on then this is a temperature list of a patient who was there for a longer period of time, say, within the war hospital, but I think that this is really the list of one of the dispensaries, because the dates are linked to the numbers here, 18, 19, 20. So these are late days. And the therapy was not urgent postoperative therapy. It is analgesics, wound dressings, and so on, and then this, this, and this temperature lists from, say, one of the other wards. Now, what follows on from this -- what follows on are copies of pages from the protocol of the war hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Starting on what date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes? Starting the 13th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One clarification, Doctor while you were speaking I was having a look at the documents. The first document concerns Delalic Aida, born in 1961, discharged on the 27th of October, apparently, temperature was 36, blood pressure 120/80. Is this the type of document that you put at the end of a bed in order to know exactly at first glance what the situation of the patient is? Because if you go to page 3 there, you have another document where you find Aida Delalic again because then she's after somebody else, and you have the feeling that this document is a document that has been drafted by the minute. At 20 hours 43, Aida Delalic, there is something mentioned, and then at 2044 there's a Peko being mentioned. So don't we have several documents that may have to do with one and the same patient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly what you mean. I can follow this in terms of dates, 15th, 16th, 17th and so on, October, up to the 20th, that is. The list on the other page, the other page is divided vertically on two sides that goes all the way up to the 26th of October. Then what we see follows on. So we had the first one, then the 27th so these are the days involved, the 31st, then the 1st, the 2nd, and so on and so forth. That's the point. And what is written down here is indeed the temperature and blood pressure, which is usually written not in millimetres but in kilopascals. Obviously that is the kind of equipment that the nurse or doctor had. So there is no special additional data provided except here it says surgeon, orthopaedic surgeon. So it was either an orthopaedic surgeon who was called in or general surgeon or the patient was taken to that person for an examination. The rest is the usual thing. So that is what hangs on the side of the bed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's what I thought. We're not going to spend hours on this, are we, Ms. Egels? Please go ahead, because I mean we've all been ill or hospitalised some day, so we know how to handle this type of document. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I just wanted the witness to see those documents and tell us if he knew about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, can I ask you to go to the third binder and to Exhibit number 3198 [Realtime transcript read in, error "3918"], please. Can you tell the trial court -- the Trial Chamber what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a photocopy of the first page, i.e., the copy page of the protocol from the Santici stationary department from the 5th of July, 1993, to 22nd -- to 20 February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, although I did not see it at the time because it was used in Santiceva stationary hospital. I didn't work there. I was there only once when this facility was being established. After that other doctors worked there. Dr. Imamovic for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I an I apologise. I believe that there has been a mistake. We have a milinfosum report which may be under seal. This is an UNPROFOR report. I believe that there has been a mistake in displaying documents on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is Exhibit 3198 and not 3918. There was a mistake on line 10, page 13. You said 3918, but as a matter of fact it is 3198.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I seem to have a problem with reading numbers these days. But I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. Thank you for the direct examination which is in keeping with expectation time wise. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the court room. If our understanding is correct as to what we've been directed to do, it's our understanding that the Trial Chamber wants the Prosecution to show the videos -- the video compilation material to this witness we're simply seeking guidance as to whether we should do that now or whether we should perhaps do that later this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. No. You are going to broadcast the video now, the one that starts with people walking on a path, and then there will be clips related to the hospital and so forth. So either you will be allowed to put further questions to the witness or the -- and the Defence will be able to cross-examine on everything that may be of interest to them, inasmuch, of course, as the witness can answer the questions. If he can't, then he won't answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps at this point it would be helpful then with the assistance of the usher if the transcripts and list indicating the exhibit numbers and time codes to be distributed at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would also ask, if I could just briefly explain to the witness what's going to happen in light of the fact that obviously -- in light of the Trial Chamber's decision, the witness is unaware of this entire procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, beforehand, Your Honour, because we are totally unaware of this procedure as well. This is the first time we are hearing this. We understood that a video was going to be played, a montage from various clips. We were not told that it was in relation to this particular witness. If I may, Your Honour. They told us they had two hours for this witness. Now this witness, through the video, it would appear they're going to take almost three hours, and I don't think -- and then are they going to be asking the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Yes. The video is exactly 58 minutes long and it relates to Mostar. It is made up of SkyNews stories, also CNN stories and BBC, HRT, ORF stories. This video compilation deals with shooting, with wounded people and people taken to places where the witness was working. So he will be able to say, "Yes, I do recognise this. This is my hospital," and that sort of thing. And it will also be possible to put questions to the witness in relation to the pictures we're going to see. So there's no surprise at all. Yesterday, the Defence counsel wanted to be able to cross-examine. There is evidence here. We have a witness. Who better than him would be able to comment on the pictures of wounded people, people who were treated there. So of course you are free to make comments, but you will do so in writing. But you know we're pressed by time and the Trial Chamber made this decision. It has been decided. We cannot go back on our decision. You will be free to cross-examine. As far as I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- there is no prejudice no harm to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, maybe I didn't -- misunderstood, maybe it wasn't translated, maybe it wasn't communicated, but I certainly never heard yesterday that they were going to be playing the video in the middle of this gentleman's testimony, and then we would be cross-examining on that part. It was my understanding that the gentleman would be testifying and that the video would be played afterwards in the event, in the event there was time left -- left to cross-examine. Now if we look at the time and today is Thursday, this gentleman was -- was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we felt and it was an option for us. But if we were to play the video after the witness's testimony, you could no longer cross-examine him on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we wanted that starting from the video --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: These decisions need to be communicated to the Defence so we can be prepared. We're hearing this for the very first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, please have a look at the transcript. Yesterday, we stated that we were going to deliberate on this issue of the video. This was written into the transcript. Yesterday we made no decision. There was an option, as was wished by the Prosecution to display or play this video later on. Mr. Kovacic got on his feet to say he didn't agree with that. We deliberated this morning, and in order to safeguard the rights of the Defence we held that the Defence, after watching this video in the presence of the witness would be free to put any questions that seem suitable to him. So this is in your own interest. I'm surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, but we want an exact accounting of all the time, and if the gentleman has to be here for the weekend so he can testify on Monday, we want our entire time. We don't want to be -- we don't want to be shortchanged because of this new approach. That's all I'm saying, Your Honour. It's Thursday today, and I just think that if the Trial Chamber is going to make decisions which I -- I'm totally in agreement with, at least we should be -- we should know about this as soon as possible so at least we would have been somewhat more prepared. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, let's stop. Let's put an end to this because we are under time pressure, and now you're slowing things down because of incidents in the proceedings. Now we're going to play the video. If the Prosecution are to have questions they can put it. I would be surprised. And then you have all the time you need until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, two facts only. It seems to me that not everything has been communicated to you. In the proofing chart that we received from the Prosecutor about witnesses, we received this one on time and nothing is mentioned about any video. Yesterday a letter arrived from the Prosecutor on the 24th of January. I don't know whether you received a copy. You should have. The Prosecutor announced yesterday and expressly said -- I'm going to read in English: "And in connection with the Mostar evidence has prepared a compilation of video material lasting approximately one hour. This presentation is a compilation of fifty media clips about Mostar from the Croatian and international media taken from the following exhibits ..." [Interpretation] This was the first time we received any notification, and there is not even a single word mentioned about the video being connected with this witness. In other words, we did not prepare to link this video with this witness. We had seen the video before because it was disclosed to us, but we have not prepared because we were not notified that it would be shown with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen, Mr. Kovacic. You said that you were not prepared but you aware of this video. You should have viewed it, and there are clips of people who were wounded, dead, or people being treated. You know that you're going to have a doctor, a surgeon, who is going to testify. Don't tell me that you didn't have any time to get yourself prepared. I don't believe this. Let's move on and play the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could just briefly explain to the witness for the benefit of his understanding. Dr. Rajkov, as you probably have followed, the Prosecution has been directed to show you this video compilation. It runs approximately one hour. We will watch these various video clips and then at the end of viewing these video clips we may have a very small number of questions for you such as, where were these videos, what's depicted in the videos, et cetera, but we don't anticipate having lengthy questions for you. Do you understand that, sir? We would then ask that the video compilation be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] He's buying time. But this is one very bloody -- and nothing can some as a surprise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[German language spoken]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] A street without a chance to escape. "On the left, the Croats. On the right, on the hills, the Serbs. The front line between Muslims and Croats runs right across the city." "[German spoken]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] People were taken to the left side. Muslims were expelled, yes. The people were taken to the left side every day. They killed many of them, up to 250 people. One of them buried without a name, with only a number. Every day they killed many of them. Cultural heritage destroyed in the Serbo-Croatian war. Merciless destruction in the Muslim cemetery next to the blown-up mosque. Cultural heritage -- the Muslims who are entrapped, they fear that there might be an agreement between the Serbs and the Croats to divide Mostar and to expel the Muslims from Mostar. In the meantime the old city has become a second Vukovar, ruins with no protection against shells and artillery attacks. The historical buildings do not have cellared walls. The old bridge is a dangerous, secret path into the Croatian part of the city. "For the Croats Mostar is the capital of their self-styled Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Bread from the west of Herzegovina for the Croats arrives. Paid for -- paid for with Croatian dinars. The products at the marketplace also come from towns in the Western Herzegovina. Before the war there were approximately the same number of Croats and Muslims living in Mostar. Muslim prisoners in the kitchen of the military prison. They're forced labourers who work for the supply of the Croatian army. We have to work in the kitchen; others have to dig trenches at the front. We have to do a lot here. The prisoners whom we film in a showpiece cell are not allowed to speak in front of the camera. Croatian retaliation for Muslim attacks against Croatian positions. We reckon that the Muslims will attempt to conquer Mostar. Since 19 April we know about the orders of their commanders, how and when this part of the city should be conquered. They never gave up this idea, and if they occupy Mostar they might have a chance to take Stolac, too, and advance further to Croatian Neum and the Adriatic Sea. The bloody conflict started in autumn of last year in the Central Bosnia -- in the Central Bosnian town of Prozor, a town with the population structure of 62 Croats [as interpreted] and 37 per cent Muslims prior to the war. Today Prozor is a -- Croatian. The UN controls a fragile cease-fire. Parts of the inner city are destroyed. Most of the Muslims from Prozor are now in Konjic. They were driven out on 28 and 29 August. I think that there were around 3.500 to 4.000 women, children, and elderly people. The men are in HVO prisons and prison camps in Capljina, Ljubuski, Mostar, and Prozor. Some were released from Jablanica. They speak of brutal maltreatment. One old man was beaten up severely so that he can hardly walk. One guy threatened to shoot him in the mouth. Those Muslim POWs were aggressors says the Croatian mayor of Prozor. The Muslims - we have documents, the Muslims had a plan to include not only Prozor but also some municipalities from Central Bosnia and Mostar into a Muslim region of Central Bosnia and Herzegovina. So they had a plan to occupy Prozor militarily. The Muslims had that plan, and the attack started in October 1992. At that time, the Muslim units, the units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were defeated. In Central Bosnia, the Croats, as the smallest ethnic group, see them receives as victims, not only from Serbian but also from Muslim attack. 180.000 people surrounded by Muslim units especially in the area of Vitez, Kiseljak, and Vares. 9.000 Croats are in prison camps. A military key position is the town of Gornji Vakuf which is fiercely embattled at the moment by Croats and Muslims. The Croatian part of the town is within firing range of Muslim snipers. Three civilians are still holding out. I still have some potatoes and flour. I cannot get into the town of the everything is closed. I don't know how it is on the other side. My house was burnt down by Muslims. Since then I've been with the soldiers. International aid is also demanded by the Croats for their people in Central Bosnia. They're bitter about the fate of their people who were displaced. While NATO is still reconnoitering over Bosnia, 3.000 metres down below the cemetery becomes too small in a war in which the victims very often are also the perpetrators."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Woman journalist: The left Muslim side for Muslims a state and for all of those who believe in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state. The Spanish Battalion is the last hope. A final link before outburst, excess, and extinction, disappearance. In the same way as Sarajevo is a symbol for Bosnia, Mostar is a symbol for a multi-ethnic community, Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Jewish tradesmen under Ottoman Empire. The destruction which was first caused by Serbs last year were driven out by Muslims and Croats has grown ten times larger since the 9th of May. Now those Croats want their part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for the Serbs, their Croat argument is clear. Where Croats live is Croat state. "'Blue Helmets': It is beautiful, Mostar, but it was devastated. This is happening because they are stupid. People kill each other here. The thing that I cannot explain to myself is, I cannot explain to myself that they fight against a country and they disagree between themselves but, at the end, let them do whatever they want. "'Blue Helmets 2': Well, no, this is not finished. There is nothing more to be done over here. We'll see. We are doing what we can do to try to make them not fight between themselves although we are still there but they don't do anything to stop. They don't want to listen to us. "Manuel Lopez: We don't know how long we will be staying here. Basically, we came here for a 24-hour guard duty. We always come here at least three times a day worth of rations and, as I already said, the situation is difficult [as interpreted]. This may result in a big mess at any moment. "Woman journalist: Didn't you recently receive special instructions exactly because there is a possibility that you might find yourselves in the situation where you have to respond on fire. "Manuel Lopez: We already know the reason why we arrived here. We are initially forbidden from responding to fire and can only do so if we are being directly shot at and we have no other way to respond, which means that we can respond only if our lives are directly threatened. Being in this type of vehicle we are not bothered by the infantry fire. However, one mortar shell, one destructive shell, can very well flatten us to the ground. If we notice any one directing that kind of weapon towards us, naturally we open fire. "Woman journalist: As Spanish troops testify daily, tragedies are lining up after the other in the face of almost general state of indifference. Like in Mostar where ethnic cleansing is still being carried out, the Croats are intimidating, expelling, or imprisoning Muslims with the aim of remaining in a purely Croat town. That man says how he was expelled last year by the Serbs in Nevesinje, Eastern Herzegovina. He fled to Mostar. Last week his younger son of 18 years of age was killed in fighting. I have another son and daughter left. I thank God because it could have been worse. Or this Bosnian soldier who is fighting for a state which everybody thinks is extinct. With some 30 or so bullets per soldier they are facing a much more numerous force, well-equipped, and in solid artillery positions which is holding them in sight from the heights just like the Serbs held them in Sarajevo. We will resist until the end, he says, we no longer believe in peace or in the Croats and we say to them that we will fight to the last man, we have nothing to lose. To isolate them even more Croats from the HVO, a paramilitary organisation, the Croatian Defence Council, trained and supported by Zagreb, are trying unsuccessfully to blow up this bridge reconstructed with humanitarian aid from the US. Due to the increasing number of conflicts along the Neretva in Herzegovina, in the zone which is in their control, in order to support them in their difficult task people who are spending entire days in their armoured vehicles without the possibility of coming out are enduring marathon shifts, 200 new soldiers, 70 logistics personnel, and 120 legionnaires have arrived from Spain as reinforcements. Since the massive house to house arrests of Muslims by the Croats from the early dawn, which began last 9th of May, and most of them are still located at the Heliodrom in Mostar the position of the Spanish blue helmets in the zone is very delicate. "Blue Helmets 3: We are currently trying to solve what we can to mediate and to try to avoid that there be further shooting but mostly we are dealing with the civilian population and refugees whom we are rescuing to ensure that people are no longer taken prisoner and to avoid being evicted from houses. "Woman journalist: While playing for time in order to maintain some sort of unstable the us quo, volcanoes of hatred are desperately erupting on both sides it was to no avail that international mediators met representatives of both sides in Medjugorje. The high-level meeting under the protection of the Spanish battalion was attended by the Bosnian and the Croatian presidents. However, the only thing that was achieved was that the importance of specific interests was highlighted, their essential disagreement. The day after the meeting in Siroki Brijeg, Franjo Tudjman, the Croatian president, paid tribute to his financiers from Herzegovina. The powerful lobby from the region had paid for his campaign and is now requesting, in exchange, to be an integral part of Croatia. Upper, where another important region occupied by the Spanish Battalion is from the Adriatic Sea towards Central Bosnia to give escort to the humanitarian aid convoys, which is deserted due to the combats, the blue helmets demonstrate their pacific orientation, already thousands times tested. Jablanica centre of the advance base is under the control of the Muslims but is surrounded by the Croats. In the field tents, Sefer Halilovic, the Bosnian military leader, and Milivoj Petkovic, the Croatian one, often discuss in the presence of the Spanish Colonel Antonio Morales. "Sefer Halilovic: It was a month ago that I asked you and have supplicated you on my knees to help us rescue the people in the mountains, both Muslims and Croats, but you negotiated with the Serbs, you did not realise that first they wanted to finish with us and then to finish with you as well. "Antonio Morales: In one or one and a half hours, already these two sides which are neutrally situated in the region, and they are EC observers and members of the Canarias Tactical Group, who will in that way return to the field to monitor what is happening in order to then be able to inform the mixed committees about what is being accomplished. "Woman journalist: There was only one opportunity to take both sides to see the devastated areas in the region only several kilometres from the base. Both sides were looking at each other with mistrust and preparing for what may follow. The Croats have tanks, mortars, people who are constantly arriving on roads which are under their control. The Muslims who have taken up positions, get weapons very rarely, and when that does happen they hurry to learn how to handle them in groups. On the other side of the mountain, Spanish blue helmets are to reduce tensions between Croats and the Muslims even though there have already been human casualties because of that. "Blue Helmets 4: Whether the memory of the lieutenant Munoz can influence us somehow when it comes to accomplish the mission. I think in reality that it doesn't, that we fulfil the mission the same as always. We take the same precautions, only when we are in the middle of some incident when the bombing or the firing is going on unconsciously always appears the image of the dead people, only when somebody dies then one takes even more precaution, hopefully, which makes us accomplish it. My friend Arturo wanted to be a legionary, he was a legionary, he lived a life of a legionary, and thank God died as a legionary. "Woman journalist: The Tactical Group Canarias Command has to calculate every patrol, escort operation, or detailed inspection reconnaissance. Every mistake could disintegrate/harm the mandate which impedes them to use the weapons only in case of legitimate defence. Lieutenant Colonel Alonso: In the remaining part of the road towards Tarcin, we have an area of conflicts in Konjic. There is a group of snipers that pound the road and do not allow the movement of vehicles, mainly civilians. They did not fire on us as yet but we have already detected reduction of civilian vehicles that move along this road in both directions. "Woman journalist: In the base in Dracevo, the Colonel Morale's men, in the beginning dedicated to control the route towards the river of Neretva, are preparing themselves continuously in the suspended mission. They clean their weapons, which they had assembled before, initiated at any time the patrol of the main corridor and the alternative accesses to Jablanica. Their plan is complex, but they have already been adapted to the place and to a conflict which, although is difficult to understand, they handled it every day with more agility."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That completes the video compilation that the Prosecution has put together. I do note the time. Perhaps it might be the appropriate moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to take a 20-minute break. We will resume at 10 past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. Before the give the floor to Mr. Mundis, there are some questions to put to the witness. Sir, after having seen the video with my colleagues, I have a few brief questions to put to you. The first one regards the conditions of life in Mostar and the second question is about the conditions in hospital. We saw people living in Mostar. On the video we saw the shelling, shots, and difficult conditions. Some people lived in basements. This, what we saw in the video, does it correspond to what you yourself experienced when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a nutshell, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My second question which is relative to the aspect for which you're here and that is the question of the hospital, the wounded, we saw on several video clips the shots that were recorded in the place when you were treating the wounded. Does this correspond to what you yourself saw and experienced? Did you recognise any of the places? Did you recognise also some of your colleagues, the wounded and those who died as a result of their wounds? Maybe you yourself recognised yourself. I don't know. Maybe you were on one of the video clips.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first thing I have to say is that, whether you believe it or not, I never saw anything of this before so I was taken by surprise. I think that on two occasions I saw myself on one of the video clips. That could have been the man in green trousers tending to somebody's leg. It is very difficult to recognise oneself. I recognised my colleague, a -- Emela Mujic. She is not a surgeon. She is a physiotherapist, and at that time she was pregnant so she couldn't do much. She even delivered her baby during the war in that hospital. I also recognised some of the nurses. Some patients I did recognise more by their diagnosis even if the names were to their faces I won recognise the names. I remember the little girl who was shot at Tekija. Her name was Selma. And as for the conditions, these conditions absolutely corresponded to what I experienced. We worked stripped to the waist because we only had two sets of surgical clothes. When one team finished two surgical procedures we had nothing else to wear. And one more remark that I have to offer, I probably did not notice all the details. There was an oxygen tank that was in one the corners. Yesterday I said that there were no gases or oxygen. It is true that there was no oxygen, but I remember that oxygen tank very well because it was obtained in a very funny way. I remember a conversation when we were discussing whether there was anywhere in the vicinity an auto mechanic that might have oxygen because their equipment also includes an oxygen tank. We asked them to bring us a tank and while we had that oxygen when -- when this was not used, it was there. Maybe somebody also noticed a radiator by a wall. The hygiene institute did have central heating installation but our repairmen, so to speak, were not very professional people. They did know something about central heating and they could never put those radiators in function. Either the radiators were out of repair or something was missing. So the radiators never worked. So during the winter it was very cold. I don't know how the patients survived all that. But as for use we were not far from comfortable. There were no windowpanes. We had some foils on the windows, and all in all that was that. That's what the condition was as it was shown on the video. And it is not without reason that everything is dark on those videos. It is not up to the cameraperson. It was really dark. There was no light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, please. I fear that there are some things in the transcript that are surprising. For instance, you have said that your mechanics were very well familiar with the equipment but they were not able to repair the radiators. Probably you wanted to say that they were not very skilful. And later on you said that you were not far from comfortable, but -- that is page 45, lines 7 and 8, but it appears in the context that you would rather want to say that you were far from comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are reading the English transcript, then you are right. I said they were not skilful. I said that they were not professionals for that kind of work. And as for being comfortable, far from it, I was not comfortable at all. Anything but that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, do you have any questions to complete your examination in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No, the Prosecution has no further questions. We believe the videotapes speak for themselves and in order to maximise the time available to the Defence we have no further questions for the witness. We would like to thank Dr. Rajkov for coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence has until 7.00. We will have a break at half past 5.00, so we have about an hour and then we will resume after the break. Who wants to start? Mrs. Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We don't have any questions for this witness. We have allocated our time -- we have given our time to the Defence of Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The following Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have also given our time to Mr. Stojic and Mrs. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't have any questions, but given that we saw the video, I think I should take the opportunity to cover some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. We saw a clip of the Security Council. Could you please tell us to what extent you were involved with negotiations or discussions at the Security Council regarding the events at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, obviously this is not the Security Council. We are not going to take into account this particular video clip when it comes to this witness. We're not going to connect the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was my whole point, Your Honour, because there are negotiations. There's fighting. There's Mujahedin. There is Vance-Owen, there's Tudjman. There's Izetbegovic. There's the peace plan. There's the Muslim plan or claim that they were trying to get to the Adriatic Sea. There's Gornji Vakuf, there's Central Bosnia, Prozor. There are all sorts of issues that were brought in, and I can go through a series of questions, and I dare say that the good doctor will tell us that he wasn't involved with any of that, including the SpaBat. I don't think that he was embedded with them, to use the term that came out of the Iraqi war, travelling with them. So he cannot tell us anything about that. And I guess the reason I want to point this out is that by bringing all this evidence in, while it may appear that we have the right to cross-examine on it and we're being afforded our right of confrontation, in actuality this is the wrong witness. And in fairness to the Defence, the Prosecution could have merely played the sections regarding the hospital and perhaps portions of Mostar. And I think that's where I think I disagree with the approach of bringing this video in at this point in time because some of those clips could have been played through various other witnesses. But if the Court is telling me that this witness is not competent to answer all of those areas that I just covered, then I'll go to the other sections that I believe the gentleman is competent to testify about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may answer Mr. Karnavas. We have discussed this. The Chamber is fully aware of what you have just exposed, but we have also seen that the range covered is so broad that probably not any single witness would have been competent to cover all the areas. We thought it's better to have one who is competent in part of it. But there remains -- there remains an open question and we grant that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, but I have to tell you, my anxiety level is way up high. I mean, I came in rather calm today but now I'm not so sure that I can maintain my equilibrium given the amount of evidence that came in through that video, much of it which was triple and quadruple hearsay. But with that qualification from you, Your Honour, I feel slightly better. Not much more, but slightly better and I'll continue now with the relevant portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, sir, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you're saying that you're feeling a bit better now and I hope that is true. You have told us that after the video I asked two very precise questions about the conditions of the life in Mostar and the hospital. I didn't ask any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it is very significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. I understand, Mr. President and I would have been -- my comfort level would have been quite better if you had just told the Prosecutor, That's all you could show. But I can understand the Court wanting to see everything because of the time constraints, and I understand and I appreciate your questions, Your Honour. They were right on target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have four points. Sir, yesterday you indicated that as of August 1992 you had a military identification card; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of August 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it was because you had that identification card that allowed you to go from the west to the east side. I believe that was your testimony yesterday, that -- correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that -- that military ID, that military identification card, was that an HVO? Was that army BiH? Was it something else?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an army of BiH ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And at the time what rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never given a rank, even after serving in the JNA. After that, I was just a foot soldier. There were no other ranks that were registered with my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you in a particular unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of any unit. I belonged to what was known at the time as a legacy of the former JNA. I was a member of the Medical Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, that would be the Medical Corps of the 4th Corps of the army of BiH? I mean, whoever was located in Mostar at the time.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that there was a system of hierarchy. It was the Medical Corps of the 1st Mostar Battalion. That's what it was known as in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, back in August of 1992, were the headquarters of the ABiH, were they in the Vranica building? You know, when you first got your identification, your military ID. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992? Truth be told, I don't know whether at the time it was at the Vranica building. Sometime later on I did go there when we were supposed to take over the signalsman when we went to the front lines. I received my ID from -- in East Mostar from one of the admin workers, if that is what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the reason I asked is because I was trying to follow your testimony from yesterday, and as I -- as I understood it, and correct me if I'm wrong or if I'm misstating anything, that on -- on May 6th you went to work and you were -- you had at that time 24-hour shifts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The shift was 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it that on the -- that on the 7th or on the 6th you might have contacted the headquarters of Vranica but it was on the 7th, on May 7th, that you spoke with an individual by the name of Ramo, I believe, who might have been your supervisor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning on the 7th of May, I spoke to the chief of the Medical Corps whose name was Ahmo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I was reading it from the transcript, but thank you for that. And that, by the way, Your Honours, can be found on page 75 to 76 of the transcript from yesterday. And I -- as I understand it, it was on the 7th that you were told that the situation was tense or -- and that best to stay on the east side; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so at least Ahmo or somebody above him knew that something was -- was in the works as early as May 7th.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, either him or somebody above him or next to him noticed or knew that the situation was not good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I take it at that point in time you didn't ask him for clarification, like what is -- what's happening? What's going to happen?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask him for a very clear reason. He informed me even earlier on when we met that we should not speak about everything on the phone because we had the same connections to the same communications centre. What I'm saying is that both the army and the HVO used the same lines of communications and that's why I was advised not to say everything on the phone or ask questions on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So when you communicated with Ahmo, this was over the telephone? Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was an induction telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, sir. So it wasn't a tete-a-tete, in other words?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And where was Ahmo at the time? Where was he located physically?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you speak to somebody on the phone, you can't be sure where that person is. Am I correct? Especially if you are not the one who dialed that other person. What I knew was that Ahmo and some of the colleagues who were in charge of the Medical Corps were in the Vranica building. When I was there they were in one part of the basement below the restaurant. They were there. So I assume that I was speaking to the man who was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you, physically, you must have been on the other side since you were finishing up your shift having started on the 6th and now this would have been I guess the morning or whatever sometime on the 7th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in the morning around 7.00 when the shifts changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you physically, I just want to make sure whether I have this picture. I'm not trying -- there are to trick questions, okay? I'm just trying to picture. Somebody is in the Vranica building we don't know but presumably somebody is there. You are finishing up your shift so you must be on the east side, okay?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the hygiene institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that person was telling you, best to stay on that side?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it you believed him. You believed him, and that's exactly what you did. You stayed on that side.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed at work and I also communicated to the others who came to replace me and the others who came to replace those others to stay put, to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Because that was -- in other words, that was the signal. I'm using this term, but that was the message to pass along to everybody, stay on -- on the east side as of the 7th of May, 1993, because the situation is tense and something may happen; right? That's a fair characterisation, would it be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you mean by signal to everybody. My work, our work, was not to inform everybody on the east side. It was just the recommendation by the chief of the Medical Corps for the Medical Corps as to what to do in the following next few days. That's what I know. That's all. The long and the short --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying was that a recommendation or was that an instruction? Because you can recommend things to somebody and the person who receives the recommendation can do whatever, and when you are instructed to do something you have to obey. So what was -- what was it that you received over the telephone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will tell you literally how it sounded. It was said, "It will be best for you to stay put. And the others who come after you should also stay there." End of quote. Those are the words and the sentences I remember very well, the couple of sentences that I really remember well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Doctor, the advice to stay there can have two motives. One is that it would be safer for you, and the other is that it is expected that a lot of work will come. You have told us that you were told it is better for you to stay there. So do I understand you correctly that you did not hear this as some sort of alarm, increased readiness, increasing the possible function of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I personally, and I repeat I personally did not perceive that as a -- as alarm. I don't know how to describe that, what word to use. I took it as advice, as a recommendation that it would be best for me to stay because of some possible events which I could not even foresee, that something would happen like it happened on the 9th of May. We were all astounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Karnavas who is asking the same questions that I wanted to ask. You are -- you have just said that something was probably going to happen, some events are expected to happen. Mr. Karnavas will explore that, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, first of all let me -- help me out here, because I'm a little confused after the last question. First you said you were instructed over the phone to be careful because you knew they were using the same phones, ABiH and HVO. So now we're talking somewhat of a coded message to you, are we not? It has a cryptic meaning to it, does it? All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say that it was a code. I apologise. Allow me to finish. This was a customary, friendly conversation that we could have had any time. The thing was that over the phone I never received any order from him in the way he is a commander and I'm a soldier obeying orders. We were just talking, and I suppose he just wanted to avoid providing specific information, military information. That is possible, but I cannot be sure of that. I was not a military unit. We did not carry arms. I was not in a position to receive any orders that I would then carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, and right now it's a little bit like trying to read the coffee cup, it seems to me, if you get my drift. But --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe that's you. Maybe you are the one who is using coffee cups. I can only tell you what I was told and it just so happens that I remember really well what was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand. And I guess the point that I'm trying -- and then, of course, you didn't -- after working 24 hours you didn't go back to the west side to at least take a shower, sleep, get some clothes, take some rest. You stayed put. You stayed on the east side and you told others to do the same; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now let me move on to the next point. And I don't presume to know a whole lot, and maybe I am reading the coffee cups, but at some point yesterday you said all of a sudden there was a -- and this was on page 96 from yesterday, that suddenly somebody unloaded a large quantity of pain-killers. It might not have been morphine, but it was pain-killers. Do you recall saying that, sir, yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, and if you want me to provide you details of that or the system of supply, I can provide you with those.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to go step-by-step.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Step-by-step.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All righty. Thank you. Now, could you tell me was that before or after this warning, this cautionary recommendation that you received. Was it before or, you know, after May 7th that somebody unloaded pain-killers. If you recall. If you don't recall, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A remark, please, if I may. I personally have the impression that you are leading me to say something that you want to prove, that you're speculating about certain things and -- allow me to finish. It was not without reason that I offered to describe our system of supplies, and if I provide you with these details, then you will be clear on how things stood. It just so happens that for that particular box of medicines --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You had a very patient and competent Prosecutor lead you through your direct. I just want to establish the point, and the point in time is when did this -- somebody unload all sorts of pain-killers? And I don't think you need to read into what I'm asking. I'm a pretty nice guy. There's nothing nefarious about my questions. I just want to know. Was it before or after May 9th? And let the Judges, they will decide what, if anything, to make with this information. Pretty straightforward

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Just like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just like that. I didn't get the --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was before. It was before the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There we go. Now we can move on to the next section, the next point.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And feel free to answer before you get the full translation, since I know you speak English. I want to talk about the generator because it kind of piqued my interest a little bit, I have to tell you. Yesterday, when you talked about this generator --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute Mr. Karnavas. I believe you will continue in the same sense but we have another problem. The questions you're asking I wanted to ask them myself and it is very well you that you have asked them. Sir, the Judges before you would like to resolve something. You're not the first witness to whom we have put such a question. We would like to know if before the 9th of May there was an attack that was staged by the BiH army against the HVO. We know that on the 9th of May it was the HVO that attacked the area under control of the BiH army, but was that attack something that was of a general nature? And yesterday you've told us that in response to the Prosecutor's question that when you were there on the 7th of May, my question was whether this was maybe mobilisation of the BiH structures because something was brewing and was envisaged to happen, because when there are preparations for an attack, the first thing that happens is that everybody is mobilised and the Medical Corps prepares drugs, medicines, and so on and so forth. You have indicated to us that you were asked to stay put, and the question is about the analgesics that were in place at the moment. My question is very simple, and I'm not going to waste any more time to put the question to you. Before the 9th of May in your knowledge, was there a plan on the part of your army, because you were a member of the BiH army, to attack the HVO troops? Was there such a plan in place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a question for a higher level, but I can say what I know, what I know. The Medical Corps, apart from what had been done, namely this recommendation advised that it would be best for you to stay there, you and the rest who are coming. That was the only thing that was done. Later on during the course of the war I had the opportunity of seeing if something was being planned somewhere that some kind of mobile groups were organised, surgery points or something like that where strikes were expected, attacks. Let me use a bit of this military terminology that I had occasion to hear then. But on the 6th, 7th, 8th, and 9th, that was not done. The only thing that was done was we should stay where we were, we from the Medical Corps. No one else did anything. After the 9th of May it seemed crazy to me, if I may use that word, that none of the military, and I saw them in the street, knew a thing. They were not getting ready for anything. They didn't know anything. It was only us there on the 6th and 7th and 8th, and I really did wonder what was going on. Why am I getting ready for something if nothing is being prepared and no one is going to do anything? That's why I said we were astounded on the morning of the 9th of May. I sincerely had the impression that we would be floored within a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course you were not one of Mr. Arif Pasalic's confidante's, were you? In other words, he didn't confide in you for -- for military advice or to tell you what would happen in advance, what he was planning? He didn't do that, did he? Just an answer, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In fact, even the lower commanders below him didn't confide in you as to what they intended to do or what they were planning on doing. They didn't say, "Hey, Doctor, let me tell you what we're about to do." They didn't say that to you. You're shaking --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly. All right. Now, let's talk about this generator. That's my last point, okay? And it seems to me, if I can recall what you said yesterday, you said even before the conflict is when you got this generator. Words to that effect. Do you recall? And I believe that can be found on page 102. That the generator came your way, this sort of Good Samaritan, if we can call him that, by serendipity just appeared and said, "Hey, by the way, there's a generator. It's up there. You know, in case you need it." And that was before the conflict. Am I characterising your testimony fairly?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Let's go step-by-step.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First, it was before the conflict? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Secondly, this gentleman just showed up and said, "By the way, there is a generator." He was an unexpected, sort of like an angel coming up -- showing up and saying, "Hey, by the way, there's a generator just in case you might need it for electricity." He just showed up uninvited, unsolicited, you know right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not say there's a generator just if you might need it. We were talking about the situation. This is a man I know by sight, and then we started talking. The idea cropped up and we actually carried it through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, hold on because I'm confused now. Yesterday you seemed to indicate that this -- that this gentleman shows up and all of a sudden springs to you this knowledge, gives you this knowledge that there is a generator that is someplace at that could be used; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was passing by there. We talked and he said that there was a generator.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And that's exactly what you said -- you said yesterday, and I'm quoting I believe on page 129 -- are we that far? 1.291. You said, "Now the electricity situation is as follows. At the very beginning, even before the conflict began, as luck would have it" - serendipity - "a man, I don't know who he was, he happened to pass by the building and met me and he said, 'Have you got a generator?'" Like I said, a good Samaritan, angel, call it whatever you want. Someone is passing by, you don't know, the timing is right, and says, "By the way," some people say "good morning," some people say, "good afternoon, how are you, how's the wife and children." He says, "do you need a generator?" Just like that.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he said good morning before he asked me that, and a few more words too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you tell us how -- how close before May 9th this might have been?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Perhaps even a month before that. That is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it could have been a few days before that as well. That's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And that generator was someplace and then you and others managed to get it down to where eventually it stayed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the situation in Mostar even at that time, about a month before, let's just say, let's just say, I'm not buying it, but let's just say it was a month before May 9th. Even a month before that time a generator of that nature, large, ability to produce lots of electricity and what have you, must have been a precious commodity. Would you agree with me on that? Precious commodity for the local government such as it was, certainly the military leaders. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN RAJKOV [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I have to say up to a point. If you have normal installations that work properly, you're not going to give it much thought. I always had the impression that over there in that situation nobody thought about the reality of war in particular. Everybody thought this is just going on for a couple of days. It's going to end. There's not going to be a war. I'm talking about 1992 onwards. This system, things will get along. That was what was wrong in our work.
